title: The New Org Chart: When AI Joins the Workforce

segments.text: Thank you so much for joining this panel. If you look at most org charts today, they were designed for a world where humans did all the thinking and
all of the typing and that world has ended 18 months ago. We've just been a little bit slow to update the diagram. I'm Damana Kazil from Dowo Jones and for
the next 30 minutes I'm joined by three leaders who are actively redrawing what a software organization looks like in AI when it's when it's actually not just a
tool but a teammate. So let me introduce them. Here to my right I have Avani Prabakar is chief people and AI enablement officer at Atlassian where
she leads people and transformation with a focus on AI fluent teams culture transformation and modern ways of working. Benjamin man is CTO at delivery
hero leading engineering teams ac across the global platform business with 25 years in technology and engineering leadership. And finally, Nilsburgger is founder and CEO of Viewpoint System, a D
tech company building smart glasses with integrated eye tracking. So, let's get to it. We have three themes to cover today and the first theme is about
redefining the work. Um, so first question for Avani, Atlassian studied six of your most AI advanced teams. What was the single biggest structural differences compared to those teams or
to the rest of the org? And was it tooling or was it something about how the work itself was organized? >> All right. Uh before I start speaking,
just want to check. Can you guys hear me all right at the back? No. Um now, can you hear me better? Is it better? Okay. All right. So, I think
it's a good sound check for all of us. we'll might have to but anyways we'll bring more energy to this room because we're talking about people and if you
can't hear us just put your hand up uh at the back uh before I answer your question um I just want to share here in
terms of you know when many of us uh read about stories in terms of AI native startup is able to do this end to end
you don't need these many people doing this I feel all of that is true but when you are in a big enterprise which is
working on like 20 year old legacy code with multiple repos with lot of complexity it's not the same for all of us so uh we call we call ourselves as
like we are brownfield but then there are also some green field initiatives so before I say in terms of uh the findings of our frontier team uh research I would
say we spent a lot of time identifying what can still qualify as a green field you know project within a big company uh so we picked up some of the initi atives
for say on Confluence. We were shipping uh Confluence slides. We were shipping some more visual features in none of our product. And the usual cycle for that
would have been about you know 16 to 20 weeks a traditional 20 member team doing the planning, review, design and then shipping. Uh we came up with some core
beliefs and some core um I would say structural changes to the team size. We said here are the green field initiatives. The team size will be not more than
five. Uh we let the team select in terms of what will be the composition of the team. So it could be all engineers based
on the feature you know product they're working on and it could be one PM one design. The team went and selected in terms of what is the construct of that
team. What we found out uh you know usually people feel uh and I'll share some outcome uh they were able to ship that feature in 2 and 1/2 weeks versus
16 weeks. So of course there was a clear kind of productivity game you you you know get the speed when you're working with smaller teams but I think the real
shift was not about the the quantum or the speed it was how they designed the redesign the way the work was happening so what I mean by that is uh it wasn't a
typical this thing as a designer was working on the prototype and then engineer was coming in and then PM they all agreed on one thing that everyone is
going to be shipping code everyone is going going to be a builder and maker in this. Everyone had to be comfortable with those blurred you know boundaries
because people get very I would say a little bit territorial to say like hey I I am an engineer if I'm accountable I don't know if I can really commit to a
you know a designer shipping a code of this quality how does that work so I think we had to change some of those norms of a working style in a team and
that's where the unlock happened. So not only did they shift faster but they redesigned the whole cycle not in terms of our traditional way how we've been
doing work. So those were some of the key uh findings. >> Thank you Avani. And Ben I know delivery hero has been moving fast on this. When
you look at team capacity now what percentage of output is AI assisted versus human only and has that changed also how you think about the team size?
So when you think about this, you need to split this in two. AI assisted and fully autonomous done via AI, right? AI assisted, it's very hard to find a team that's not
using AI every day in all parts, right? How they design things, how they think about architecture, how they write code, how they review code, how they deploy
it, how we handle incidents, it's in every step of that funnel, right? Now, how we do this? We give teams great autonomy to pick kind of what works for
them because we have the luxury also having a very distributed engineering team. So we can do a lot of organizational AB tests. What works in
team one may not work in team two, right? And we're seeing good results with this one. We're going really fast and we want teams to use this every day.
Not because we dramatically look at adoption as a metric. I think adoption is a pretty lame metric but it's a good proxy metric to surface where we find
the work needs to change right so when we look across teams and we see certain teams are struggling to incorporate these technologies in their incident
response we always uncover okay it's a tooling problem it's an adoption problem it's a skill problem that we need to fix so we use adoption as a metrics to
surface where do we need to deep dive and equip teams to be better with it. Right? So the second part is how much of
the work, how much additional work we want to create fully autonomous. There we're going slower and right now it's around probably 10 to 15% of all the work that we do is done
fully autonomous. Um we're going intentionally slow because as we ramp this up, we find three things. First of all, it's a skill issue that we still
need to address, right? People need to learn new technologies and we need to teach them how to do this safely. Second, if you work with large code base
and large distributed architectures, not all areas are ready to do this and and and to accept this. And third, as we go through this journey, we uncover what
guard rails we are missing, right? And that's usually a bit of a painful lesson to learn, right? Because you know that you miss a guard rail once you know that
you miss a guardrail. So there we're going a bit more slower and see okay what works what do we need to change how we think about the work in itself before
we push this to the next level. Thank you, Ben. And Neil's moving to deep tech. The work includes things that AI can't easily touch, maybe hardware
constraints, physics, safety. How do you decide which parts of your engineering workflow to hand to AI and which ones stay human only? >> Trial and error.
>> Um, I envy you folks that you have clear strategies. I don't. Um, I think that's the beauty of AI. At the same time, it's
the challenge. Um, it's very tricky to wrap your head around at really setting milestones and targets. I can't. If you can, well done. Let's have a chat
afterwards. Um, with us as an embedded company, there is hardware involved. So, that's a whole different animal again. Um, there is currency, there is
battery, so safety standards. So we just can't unleash it as others might come out to ship a demonstrator. So for us different sets of rules apply
to certain extent. Yes in the software stack we are quicker but in general um it will have an impact but currently it's trial and error and uh uh it's us
then discussing what does make sense what not and when do we circle back to it try it again. if something has changed. So yeah, um boring, [laughter]
>> not at all. So now moving on to the second theme, the evolution of talent, the junior to senior pipeline. The thesis is if AI handles entry-level code
generation, then the traditional apprenticeship model breaks. The junior to senior pipeline is at risk and middle management needs reinvention. Ben, so it's an understatement.
>> Strong ones. Yes. Um, so first of all, I think companies that stop investing in entry-level talent deserve to go out of business. I have no data to back that
up, but it's a strong belief that I hold and it's a strong belief that we hold as a company also at delivery hero. Right.
Second of all, a big part of that thesis is the assumption that the work of entrylevel engineers is less valuable and less complex and hence easier to
replace. I challenge that assumption also because that's only true if you make the big mistake of hiring someone at the beginning of their career and then
excuse the language put them at the most job that you can find that no one else wants to do right I think that's a
travesty if you do this as an organization so we designed our entire program on how we intake young engineers and how we intake people at the
beginning of their careers is that our mission is from day one we want to put these people at the beginning of their year of their career at some of the
hardest things that we have, right? Because we hire them because we believe in their future growth potential and we believe that the skills that they need
to work on these areas we can teach and we are very successful with this. We continue to hire entry-level talent. We continue to hire career switches. We
continue to invest in our internalmies that we have all over the world. Seoul, Berlin Korea Barcelona Singapore. There's large programs that we run to
ensure that we become that we stay a company that as the work of a software engineer changes that we teach the right skills to the next generation of
software engineers. But so what does the junior developer actually do dayto-day in a world where co-pilot writes the boiler plate? What are you hiring for?
>> So what we hiring good output >> so what we are hiring for it's again that has not changed when we hire for especially at the entry level we look
for people that are smart that are curious that want to learn that want to grow that have big ideas of things that they want to build. we hire for builders
and to to use a a phrase. Now what has changed is what do we need to teach them in addition to the traditional skills that every software
engineer needs to have because you still need those skills even if AI writes the code. You still need to understand whether that code is good. You still
need to understand how you write codes and how do you design systems that scale across billions of orders and billions of transactions. So that skill set has
not changed. What's added to is okay with these new technologies how do you use them? How do you learn? How do you train them? How do you optimize
performance versus cost? So the entire AI skill set which is like a I haven't found a better phrase for it um becomes an additional pillar in our software
engineering career framework that we we find is our job as a company to teach to everyone not just young talent at the beginning of their career but also to
principal engineers that are 20 years as software engineers because they lack these skills also in certain areas >> and Neils let's talk about the middle
management squeeze. So in your world, the team lead used to be a person who tracked tasks and unblocked PRs. What does that role become when AI handles a
lot of the coordination layer? >> I would call it an empathy layer. Um those humans they have now to pick up other tasks because certain things go more
automated. You have less interaction. You're now talking to an AI. So I think the the the the major driver behind being a good team
lead is connecting the dots, figuring out who is getting lost by just getting too focused, too narrow-minded and being dragged in by the AI. By the way, that's
kind of a similarity towards social media. The more you put in, the more you get out trending towards a certain topic. So those people that there is a
huge opportunity but it in my opinion it won't be skilldriven like I'm extremely good in XY Z you need to be capable of connecting the dots to have the full
picture. So basically it's not a squeeze you get more pressure because usually the headoffs that was their field and that layer goes down a bit. So
we expect more from the team leads in managing really people and not taking technical decisions. >> And Aani does this resonate at Atlassian scale.
>> So on uh both the topics of grad and middle management our take is I feel like everyone seems to be rushing to make bold statements
and I'm with you Benjamin on this to say hey we won't need grad like all of that. I again say it's like lot of
out there. Everyone is just trying to make bold statements about org structure, future of manager, future of grad, future of sui as a job family
where with a they haven't done real research behind it. So what we have been doing is uh we have a small team it's called teamwork lab. It's a team of
behavioral scientists. They are just researching every job family and we publish out research on each and every job family. I know most of you here are
sui and sui happens to be the most of the most talked about jobs that are being impacted by AI. So I think what we
have done is we have rewritten in terms of what does the job spec look like for a suite. You have to start from there
that the work is shifting from code generation to write of code which means you require more engineering expertise. is you require more engineering depth to
really understand if this code written by AI is is is is is ready to be shipped or not. So I feel like that's the part
that we should be talking about but people choose to talk about more less future all of that stuff. So that's one when it comes to grad again 110% you
know in agreement with Benjamin and I like the passion I feel like the companies who would not invest in their early in career right now will have no
future. So that's one in terms of what we have seen the shift is uh the universities I feel like we need to take a step back right now the education
system hasn't really caught up completely in terms of what should a true AI native grad look like coming out of uni so I think the work that we are
doing is working with some of the core universities in terms of really working with them in the last 6 months of graduation to say what is what should
they actually incorporate in their study curriculum so that when they come out of uni they have a different skill set. Uh we have also fine-tuned our selection
criteria completely. So we have an intern program and that's our internal pipeline for grad. So we get to spend about three months with them and we have
completely changed our intern program to make sure that we are really kind of upskilling them but also assessing the the AI native u you know skills there
and our research the reason why we are so bullish on hiring grads is because we researched our own grads right now and we studied their output their output uh
was 20% more super users were coming from that population as compared to the other cohort that's one when you see how they use AI for decision-m they are 2x
more productive than rest of the population so you have to kind of have your thesis build on some research so that's all on grad
middle management again everyone wants to say you will not require managers or the span of control will go this or like you know all of that is again a lot of
AI washing as I call it I feel like the role of manager is going to become even more and more important important because you're talking about
traceability, you know, accountability, what happens when there's an incident management, you still need a human at the end of the chain who is accountable
for all of that stuff. What we are seeing is the role is pivoting dramatically. Uh they need to really spend a lot of time in building the
context layer, what we call as the knowledge graph or teamwork graph to make sure that there's enough data layer they've built for our agents and human
to work side by side. So the role is again evolving dramatically. We do expect them to be 80% of the time being a player and 20% coach. So managers who
were just doing performance reviews and just coaching I think that type of management is shifting but it has to be more ICE technical depth senior leaders
>> and actually Ben I know that delivery hero your career framework has been through three versions in nine months at least. How do engineers react when the
goalpost keeps moving? >> Actually, they love it because they're the ones changing the goalpost, right? Our engineering career framework is not a stone tablet that we hand down from
the top. It's completely crowdsourced by a group of 10, 20, 30 people in engineering that give us as executives and leaders the right input. We see
changes in technologies, shifts in the way of working from the ground up that we think okay we need to make this a more integral part of our career
framework because we see more weight and more dependency and gaps in our current workforce right so we go through three big ones but also like minor adjustments
three or four times in a year because it's for all of our tech families completely crowdsourced by the people that know best the ones that do the job
right and and HR comes in also as a partner to say okay this is how it fits into leveling promotion criterias and so on right but the actual meat the content
of our career frameworks is driven by IC1 so entry- level people to principal engineers engineering managers to SVPs of engineering it's a pretty diverse
group from all over the world that inputs into this >> and Avani you just spoke about AI super users and I know that that's also
changed at Atlassian, what you meant maybe three times in 18 months and that you're also about to release an AI transformation playbook. Walk us through that evolution
of the AI super users. I would say uh the reason I I mean I'm happy to share that example is because everyone here should go in on the AI
transformation journey with one belief that no one knows what the hell we are working on right now. and just be honest about it. I feel like lot of senior
leaders have the pressure to say like we know what we're doing or we are the first one to do it or like all of that.
I feel like if you start from a place of humility to say we don't know, we will learn as we go along the journey is a
good grounding start for any leader sitting out here on this journey. For us, we learned it also the same way. uh when we started uh on the AI adoption
journey we were in initially tracking just the adoption of 1 P 3P tools and we realized in 3 months everyone because you are a tech product tech company
everyone was like 90% usage and it so and we were like so what like you are using AI but did not know what is it
really meant for the company then we pivoted it to uh to a definition of super user being if you're using 40 times a more advanced feature in AI to
make an actual decision then we qualify you as a super user. Then we started tracking super users. Uh now we are at third stage where we are defining what a
super user looks like in engineering craft versus a salesperson. You know an engineer uses AI very differently to how a salesperson is using it right now. So
we're kind of defining that for an individual craft level and trying to track that. I don't think so we are there as yet where we can say like hey
we can measure the output to say like hey what did it deliver because all the output metrics right now for AI are very productivity our product code gen went
up by x% our PR cycle time has reduced all of those metrics doesn't really give you any indication of so what as an enterprise you know just because you can
ship more code doesn't mean that the whole SDLC is like that much more effective we are not there at the journey of transformation. So that's how
we are approaching it and learning it. And I would say the stage four of would be once we know a real output gain is
when we'll start measuring that. >> And Neils in deep tech, the human element isn't just about feelings or empathy like you mentioned earlier, but
it's also about accountability. So when I contribute to a system that interacts with the physical world, who owns the output and how do your engineers think
about that? Um that's a very important topic um especially in our domain um because we're not doing smart classes we're also we developed a human machine interface
and it has to work and I have to sign at the end of the development circle with my name that this has been done with to
the point where it's shippable. So and then comes AI which I think doesn't take any accountability. So I think you mentioned we're doing a lot with the
ministries of defense. There is also about always about human in the loop. Um and that's also concept we are following. So that means everything we
do has a human in the loop and needs to be at the end of the day cleared for the next stage by a human being. That can be
a highly qualified software guy that really checks whether what we did together with AI really meets meets our own ambitions. But at the same time, I never thought I
would use that phrase, but there needs to be some regulation because we are struggling. Um, and no one tells us how we can overcome
a struggle by not knowing what what do we have to unveil, what we have to give more transparency. So, I'm not a huge fan of regulation. Uh but here honestly
us as a as a hardwardriven company we are struggling like hell and accountability to answer the question you want is really down to a human being
and honestly at the end of the day that's me. So yes I'm a huge fan of accountability. [snorts] >> Thank you so much. And here's what
strikes me of the last 25 minutes. I think we have three very different organization. 20,000 person platform company, a global delivery marketplace and a deep tech
hardware software shop. And I think we're all landing on the same truth that maybe AI is the easy part. And that managing the cultural and human shift,

redesigning teams, rethinking talent pipelines, keeping engineering feeling less like a function, more like craft people rather than reviewers. That's an infinitely larger engineering challenge than the technology itself.
So, thank you so much to our panel. Um, and I would like to open up and see if there are any questions. >> Yes, there are several questions. The
first one is by Lee Young. Um, this is for the whole panel, so feel free to to jump in. Entrylevel rules are becoming less and less. How do we build the next
generation of workforce if we cannot develop a generation who can detect the flaws and have critical thinking from AI output? Well, do you do you do do you agree with
the statement that entry jobs are becoming less and less? >> So, I see it as a trend in the industry. As I said before, I think it's a stupid
trend. Um, and I agree with the concern. Our approach is to ensure that these entry-level jobs do not become less and less because we are teaching
organization. I think everyone should do that. But I agree with a trend in the industry. I just think it's stupid. >> Uh one thing I would say is currently I
think people are putting lot more energy in in the volume to say we need less or more. I think the energy should shift in. So if you currently a grad comes in
they take about 2 years to get to from a you know entry- level engineer to the next level. But what what we should be
focusing is how can we amplify that you know learning curve from 2 years to one year time frame. So you still hire the uh you know this thing but invest in all
the critical thinking that you're talking about. The biggest worry is how do you train them if they haven't spent years to really understand where where
does AI start hallucinating if this code because most of the engineering bandwidth right now is being spent on write off code like I said in terms of
reviewing doing the code review you can only do that if you have the context and the years of experience and the depth to do that so I feel where we are spending
our energy is like that's a good problem to solve how do you solve it with AI so that if I'm a grad coming in. I don't
have to really spend 10 years to get to that level of experience. Can I do that in 5 years time? I think that's the
problem to solve rather than saying that they won't be able to do it and hence the solution is not hire grads. >> How's that at Dow Jones?
>> Similar. I think we're struggling still with the career framework, relooking at our job descriptions. I think we're looking we're looking to try and be

>> Um, we don't do that. I don't understand the question. Great talent is great talent. uh if you find great talent, hire him or her and then evolve into the
position you see them. Uh for us uh it's the it's not the only denominator is not AI. It's one fraction of what we do
